results.summary: This project is a Wokwi design that changes lights when buttons are pressed, according to its one-line description and how-it-works text. The documentation is extremely thin: there is no explanation of the logic, no details on how to test beyond "Not really sure", and no external hardware listed. The pin names ui[0] and ui[1] as inp0/inp1 and uo[0]/uo[1] as out0/out1 suggest simple input-to-output connections, but the actual behavior is unclear. The project appears to be a placeholder or incomplete experiment with insufficient information to describe its function accurately.

This project implements a 3-bit arithmetic logic unit (ALU) that performs arithmetic and logical operations on two 3-bit binary numbers, selected by two select lines. It is built in Wokwi and uses eight inputs: six for operands a and b, and two for the operation select. The outputs drive a seven-segment display to show the result, with the display exhibiting a random sequence on startup until the circuit settles after two clock cycles. External hardware required is a seven-segment display, and the design serves as an educational example of a basic ALU.

This design implements a simple 2-input AND gate, with inputs connected to ui[0] and ui[1] and the output to uo[0]. It is built in Wokwi and can be tested by toggling the inputs in binary order (00, 01, 10, 11) and observing the output, which should only be high for input combination 11. The project appears to be a basic logic gate demonstration or template, with no external hardware required. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand the function.

This project is a placeholder from a Tiny Tapeout workshop, with a one-line description that says "Not sure yet but yeah" and no meaningful documentation. The how-it-works and how-to-test sections are generic instructions to explain well, and the external hardware field mentions "lots of hardware" without specifics. The design has no pin definitions and no clear function, making it impossible to describe what it does beyond being an incomplete workshop exercise. There is essentially no documentation.

This is a small test design named "chip one" that includes logic gates, with outputs labeled "output or" and "output and" suggesting OR and AND functions. It has eight inputs (a, b, c, e, f, g, h, i) and two outputs; the how-it-works and how-to-test sections both say "Click the switches to see different parts light up" followed by arbitrary numbers. The documentation is sloppy and incomplete, with no clear explanation of the internal logic or expected behavior. It appears to be a rudimentary experiment, likely from a workshop, with no external hardware listed.

This project, titled "Tiny Tapeout Workshop by Kirsty Tan", has a one-line description that describes Tiny Tapeout itself rather than the design. The documentation consists of placeholder text "ffff" and "ff", and pin names are generic (Inputa through Inputh, Outputa through Outputh). There is no explanation of functionality, testing, or external hardware, other than "List sers" which appears to be a typo. The design is effectively undocumented and appears to be a workshop template or incomplete entry.

This design, called "Tiny tapeouts test gates", displays the letter H on a BCD display when all inputs are set to 1. It uses inverters on two pins to change their values from 1 to 0, forming the pattern needed for the letter H on a seven-segment display. The output pins are configured to drive the display segments, with specific pins set high or low; for example, OUT0 and OUT3 are 0 while others are 1. The project is a simple test of logic gates and display driving, requiring a seven-segment display as external hardware.

This project is described as a D-type flip-flop, though the documentation also mentions an AND gate and an inverter, suggesting a mix of logic elements. It has eight inputs: inputs 1 and 2 feed an AND gate, and the rest connect directly to a display, with the final display input being an inverted version of input 2. The outputs drive a seven-segment display, and the design can be tested by toggling the switches to observe the logic gate behavior. The documentation is somewhat unclear and the clock is set to 10 Hz, indicating a simple educational experiment with external hardware likely being a seven-segment display.

This design tests various logic gates (NOT, NOR, OR, XNOR) and a clock divider to produce the letter Y on a seven-segment display when the inputs are set to 00101110. It has eight inputs and eight outputs, with some outputs sharing names like OUT1 and OUT6 appearing twice, which may indicate a wiring mistake or intentional duplication. The primary function is to demonstrate gate combinations and display control, and it requires an external seven-segment display. The design is an educational test of basic digital logic and clock division.
